title: Five people who work night shifts

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: Speaker one.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I work nights at a twenty-four-hour pharmacy. When my twins started school, my husband and I worked out that if I took nights, one of us would always be at home with them. That's the whole reason.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The money is a bit better, I suppose, but not much. And staying awake isn't really the problem. By three in the morning, the adrenaline kicks in.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: What wears me down is the people who come in at that hour. Some are frightened, some are rude, and a few have clearly been drinking. You have to stay calm and polite, and after ten hours that's exhausting. Last month a man shouted at me for twenty minutes about the price of cough sweets.

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: Speaker two.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: I'm a lab technician at a hospital. During the day, the lab is chaos. Phones ringing, people walking in with questions. On nights, it's just me and the machines, and I can finally think properly.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: That's why I asked for the transfer. A colleague assumed I wanted to escape my boss, but I actually get on well with her. She's the one who signed the form, and she still checks how I'm doing.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: The hardest part is social. My friends meet up on Friday evenings, and I'm always at work. I've missed birthdays, and even a wedding. You start to feel as if life is happening somewhere else, without you.

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: Speaker three.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I drive a delivery lorry. Nights pay almost a third more, and with a mortgage, that decided it for me. The roads are quieter too, which is a bonus, but I'd do it in heavy traffic for that money.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I sleep fine, honestly. Blackout curtains, earplugs, done. What I find hard is my parents. They ring me at eleven in the morning and sound hurt if I don't answer.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: My mother still tells people I've got a temporary job, after six years. It's as if they think I'm just being lazy all day.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I've tried explaining that eleven in the morning is my three in the morning. They nod, and then they ring again the next day. I've stopped arguing about it.

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: Speaker four.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: I'm a night porter at a hotel while I finish my law degree. Lectures are in the mornings, and seminars in the early afternoon, so working nights was the only way to fit everything in.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: The shift is mostly quiet. The odd guest arrives late and complains about something, but that's rare, and it's never serious.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: My problem is sleeping. I share a flat above a café, and from about eight in the morning there's the coffee machine, the deliveries, the chairs scraping on the floor. I sleep in pieces, two hours here, an hour there.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: I've tried earplugs and a fan, but nothing really works. Moving out isn't an option until I graduate.

segments.speaker: N
segments.text: Speaker five.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: When I qualified as a nurse, I applied everywhere. The only post that came up was on the night team at a care home, so I took it. I thought I'd move to days after a year, but I've stayed.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I don't mind the darkness. I've never been a big fan of sunshine anyway. And the drive home at dawn is actually quite peaceful.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The thing I can't get right is food. Is a meal at two in the morning lunch or dinner? I either eat nothing, or I snack on biscuits all night, and my body really doesn't thank me for it. I keep promising myself I'll bring a proper meal in a box. So far, that's lasted about three days.

task1.prompt: Task 1: Why did each speaker start working nights?

options.B: They wanted to avoid heavy traffic.
options.C: They could share childcare with their partner.
options.D: A colleague asked them to swap shifts.
options.E: It allowed them to study during the day.
options.F: It was the only job available to them.
options.G: They wanted to get away from their manager.
options.H: They could concentrate better at night.

task2.prompt: Task 2: What does each speaker find most difficult about working nights?

options.C: staying awake in the early hours

explanations1.en: She took nights so that 'one of us would always be at home' with the twins: 'That's the whole reason' (C). The money is 'a bit better... but not much' (not A).
explanations1.cs: Rozhodla péče o děti sdílená s manželem. Vyšší plat zmíní, ale zlehčí ho ('not much').

explanations1.en: By day the lab is chaos; at night 'I can finally think properly. That's why I asked for the transfer' (H). A colleague thought he wanted to escape his boss, but 'I actually get on well with her' (not G).
explanations1.cs: Důvodem je klid na soustředění. Útěk před šéfovou je domněnka kolegy, kterou mluvčí vyvrací.

explanations1.en: 'Nights pay almost a third more... that decided it for me' (A). Quieter roads are 'a bonus', and he would work 'in heavy traffic for that money' (not B).
explanations1.cs: Rozhodly peníze ('that decided it'). Prázdnější silnice jsou jen bonus navíc, ne důvod.

explanations1.en: With lectures in the mornings, 'working nights was the only way to fit everything in' while finishing his degree (E). 'The only way' refers to his timetable, not to a lack of other jobs (not F).
explanations1.cs: Noční směny mu umožňují studovat přes den. Pozor: 'the only way' neznamená jediné volné místo (F), ale jediný způsob, jak skloubit práci a studium.

explanations1.en: 'The only post that came up was on the night team, so I took it' (F). She stayed later by choice, but that was not why she started.
explanations1.cs: Nastoupila, protože nic jiného nebylo k dispozici. To, že zůstala, je až pozdější rozhodnutí.

explanations2.en: 'What wears me down is the people who come in at that hour' – frightened, rude or drunk customers (G). 'Staying awake isn't really the problem' (not C).
explanations2.cs: Nejtěžší jsou nepříjemní zákazníci. Udržet se vzhůru výslovně problém není – distraktor C je popřen.

explanations2.en: 'The hardest part is social... I've missed birthdays, and even a wedding' (B). The chaos he mentions is about day shifts, not his main difficulty.
explanations2.cs: Trpí tím, že mu uniká společenský život s přáteli ('life is happening somewhere else').

explanations2.en: 'What I find hard is my parents', who think his job is 'temporary' and that he is 'lazy all day' (E). He says 'I sleep fine', so D is wrong.
explanations2.cs: Problémem je postoj rodičů, kteří jeho práci neberou vážně. Spánek mu nevadí ('I sleep fine').

explanations2.en: 'My problem is sleeping', because of the café below: the coffee machine, deliveries and scraping chairs (D). Complaining guests are 'rare' and 'never serious' (not G).
explanations2.cs: Nemůže spát kvůli hluku z kavárny. Stěžující si hosté jsou výjimka, proto G nesedí.

explanations2.en: 'The thing I can't get right is food... I either eat nothing, or I snack on biscuits all night' (A). She does not mind the darkness (not F) and finds the drive home 'peaceful' (not H).
explanations2.cs: Neumí si nastavit rozumné časy jídla. Tma ani cesta domů jí nevadí – obojí zazní jako past.
